# Introduction {.section-slide visibility="uncounted"}

Section 02 / 07

## What's Regional Favoritism? {.content-slide}

The tendency of national leaders to direct disproportionate public resources toward their own birth region, rather than allocating them on the basis of need or national interest.


### How It's Measured {.larger}

- Compare a leader's birth region against all other regions of the same country, in the same year
- Use satellite-recorded nighttime light intensity as a proxy for local economic activity
- Ask whether the birth region gets systematically brighter while its leader is in power

::: {.notes}
Regional favoritism is when leaders steer resources toward their own
birth region, not where they're most needed. 

Government spending data can't
test this, it's missing or unreliable exactly where favoritism would
matter most, so we use nighttime light as a proxy instead. It's
satellite-measured, the same method everywhere, and no government can
edit it.

We compare a leader's birth region to other regions in the same country and year, and ask whether it gets brighter while that leader is in power.
:::



## An Example: Ivory Coast {.content-slide .figure-slide}

::: {.case-study-figure}
![](img/goh_combined.svg)
:::

::: {.notes}
Here's one concrete case. This is Gôh in Ivory Coast, the birthplace of
Laurent Bqagbo, who took office in 2000. The dashed line is the country
average, and the solid line is Gôh. They track closely through the
nineteen nineties, and then right at 2000 they split apart. Gôh pulls
away from the national average and keeps climbing, while the rest of the
country stays flat.

You can see it in the maps too. Watch the lit area right inside the
region's boundary get thicker and brighter across those four years. 
:::



## The Paper We Replicate {.content-slide .paper-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Hodler & Raschky (2014), *Quarterly Journal of Economics*

::: {.fact}
[Research question]{.fact-label}

Do national leaders steer resources to the region they were born in? And if so,
how far does the effect reach geographically, how long does it last, and where is
it worst?
:::

::: {.fact}
[Sample]{.fact-label}

**38,427 subnational regions in 126 countries**, observed annually from
**1992 to 2009**, covering the entire usable DMSP-OLS satellite nighttime light record at the time.
:::

::: {.fact}
[Empirical Strategy]{.fact-label}

The outcome is nighttime light intensity. A region is treated in the years its
country's effective leader was born there. Region and country-year fixed effects
hold the comparison **within country, within year**.
:::

::: {.fact}
[Finding]{.fact-label}

Birth regions are about **4% brighter** while their leader is in office. The
effect is strongest where institutions are weak and education low, and it is
amplified by foreign aid and oil rents [@hodler2014].
:::

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

::: {.paper-cover}
![](img/hr2014_cover.png)
:::

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the original paper authored by Hodler and Raschky, in Quarterly Journal of Economics, in 2014. 

Their panel covers
38,427 regions in 126 countries, 1992 to 2009, basically the full
usable DMSP satellite record at the time.

The outcome they use is nighttime light intensity. Their empirical
strategy controls for two things. It controls for anything that never
changes about a place, and it controls for anything that hits the whole
country at once in a given year. So what's really being compared is
one region against the rest of its own country, in that same year.

Headline number is four percent brighter. It's strongest where
institutions are weak and education is low, and it grows with aid and
oil money, so favoritism needs both a motive and the means.

My job was to reproduce this first, then push the data past 2009.
:::

## Literature {.content-slide .lit-slide}

::: {.columns-2}
::: {}
::: {.col-heading}
Foundational
:::

::: {.lit-entry}
[Measuring Economic Growth from Outer Space]{.lit-title} [[@henderson2012]]{.paper-cite}

- **Data:** Nighttime lights matched to national GDP growth, cross-country panel
- **Scope:** Validating satellite light growth as an economic-activity proxy
- **Finding:** Light growth is an **independent proxy for GDP growth** that outperforms official statistics where national accounts are weak
:::

::: {.lit-entry}
[Distributive Politics Around the World]{.lit-title} [[@golden2013]]{.paper-cite}

- **Data:** Review of the distributive-politics literature, no single dataset
- **Scope:** How political favoritism has been measured across countries
- **Finding:** Prior work relied almost entirely on **single-country spending data**, leaving systematic cross-country evidence largely absent
:::
:::
::: {}
::: {.col-heading}
Related / Extensions
:::

::: {.lit-entry}
[Does the Leader's Ethnicity Matter?]{.lit-title} [[@franck2012]]{.paper-cite}

- **Data:** Demographic and Health Surveys, Sub-Saharan Africa
- **Scope:** Ethnic favoritism in health and education outcomes
- **Finding:** Districts sharing the president's ethnicity see **relative gains in education and child mortality** while that leader is in power
:::

::: {.lit-entry}
[Birthplace Favoritism Revisited]{.lit-title} [[@bora2025]]{.paper-cite}

- **Data:** VIIRS nighttime lights, 2012-2025, matched to PLAD birthplaces and GADM boundaries
- **Scope:** Robustness of birthplace favoritism in the modern, high-frequency era
- **Finding:** Favoritism starts **immediately on taking office** and persists after leaving it, with a further premium during COVID-19 in weaker democracies
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Four papers to place this project on the map.

Two are foundational. Henderson, Storeygard and Weil is the paper that made
nighttime lights usable for economics in the first place: they show that the
change in light output tracks GDP growth well enough to substitute for official
statistics, which matters most exactly where those statistics are worst. 

Golden
and Min then surveyed the distributive-politics literature and found the field
had been stuck at single-country spending data. That gap is precisely what
Hodler and Raschky's satellite approach was built to close.

The other two push on the mechanism and the modern data. Franck and Rainer use
household survey data across Sub-Saharan Africa and find the same logic one
level down: districts that share the president's own ethnicity see real gains
in health and education outcomes while that leader is in power. 

And Bora
pushed into the VIIRS era, with monthly rather than annual data, and found two
things I did not expect: the effect shows up immediately when a leader takes
office rather than with a lag, and it spiked again during COVID, concentrated
in weaker democracies.

That last point is a nice preview of where my own extension is headed.
:::

# Empirical Framework {.section-slide visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.section-eyebrow}
Section 05 / 07
:::


## Empirical Framework {.content-slide .eq-slide}

<div class="eq-block">
$$
\text{Light}_{ict} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \beta_{ct} \;+\; \gamma\,\text{Leader}_{ict-1} \;+\; \varepsilon_{ict}
$$
</div>

::: {.fact}
[The Variables]{.fact-label}

- $\text{Light}_{ict}$ is log nighttime light intensity(<code>log(light + 0.01)</code>) for region $i$,
  country $c$, year $t$ .
- $\text{Leader}_{ict-1}$ is 1 if region $i$ was the effective leader's birth
  region in $t-1$, 0 otherwise.
:::

::: {.fact}
[Fixed Effects, $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_{ct}$]{.fact-label}

- $\alpha_i$ absorbs everything **time-invariant** about a region.
- $\beta_{ct}$ absorbs every **national shock common to a country-year**.
- What survives is variation **within region, within country, within year**.
:::

::: {.fact}
[Coefficient of Interest, $\gamma$]{.fact-label}

- HR expect and find $\gamma > 0$: a **positive, significant $\gamma$** is
  read as evidence of regional favoritism.
- Standard errors are **clustered by leader**, lagged one period for
  consistency with $\text{Leader}_{ict-1}$ itself.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is HR's own equation. The dependent variable is log light. They
add a small constant, 0.01, before taking the log, because a lot of
regions record zero light in a given year, and you can't take the log
of zero, so that constant keeps those unlit regions in the sample
instead of dropping them. 

The variable we care about is Leader, lagged
one year, whether that region is the current leader's birthplace.

Region fixed effects control
for anything permanent about a place, and country-by-year fixed effects
control for anything national that hits every region at once. 

What's
left is one region against the rest of its own country, in the same
year. Authors expect a positive and significant value of 𝛾
, which is read as evidence of regional favoritism.
:::

Standard errors are adjusted for leader clustering. \*\*\*, \*\*, \* indicate significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.</p>

<div class="cmp-callout">Sample restricted to HR's exact <strong>126-country, 1992-2009</strong> window. Column (8) uses G-Econ 4.0, our substitute for HR's own Gennaioli et al. (2014) source, which was never publicly released. All eight <strong>Leader</strong> coefficients match HR's sign; Column (6) <strong>loses significance</strong> in our panel (0.014, not significant, vs. HR's 0.029***). <strong>Pop</strong>'s sign flips in Columns (7)-(8), a genuine population-source difference (GPWv4 vs. HR's CIESIN vintage), not a bug.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is HR's own Table II, eight columns, each one split into their number
and ours side by side, run through our own pipeline on their exact sample.
Let me walk through the eight quickly.

Column one is the headline result, one year lag, and we get 0.037 against
HR's 0.038, both significant. 

Having a leader originate from a region (a shift from $0$ to $1$) is associated with approximately a 3.7% increase in nighttime light intensity 

Columns two and three just change the lag,
current year and then a two year lag, and the estimate barely moves, so
the result isn't sensitive to that choice. 

Column four adds last year's
light level as a control and the coefficient shrinks a bit but survives.

Column five drops region fixed effects entirely and the coefficient gets
larger, which is expected, their main specification is the conservative
one.

Column six is the one place we don't fully match HR, it drops the log
constant, and ours comes out small and not significant where theirs is
significant, so I'm flagging that honestly rather than hiding it.

Column
seven switches to light per capita and column eight switches to regional
GDP using G-Econ, our substitute for HR's own data source, and both hold up
in sign and significance.

Population's sign flips in the last two columns,
that's a real difference between population datasets, not a bug.

:::

<script>
// Plain global functions wired via inline onclick="" rather than
// addEventListener/querySelectorAll -- simpler and doesn't depend on any
// class-based element matching still being intact after Pandoc/Quarto's
// own HTML post-processing of this table (which is known to strip
// class="" from raw <img> tags inside table cells elsewhere in this
// deck; using onclick="" here sidesteps that class of problem entirely).
// reveal.js's Speaker View opens the deck a second time in a popup
// window (its "current slide" pane is a live iframe of this same page,
// not a static mirror). A click there runs this script in THAT window's
// own document only -- classList changes stay local to whichever window
// received the click, so opening a lightbox from the popup never touched
// the real, audience-facing main window. Fixed by broadcasting every
// open/close over postMessage to the opener (or, from inside the notes
// popup's iframe, window.top's opener) so both sides mirror each other.
function erdoganFindOpener() {
  try { if (window.opener) return window.opener; } catch (e) {}
  try { if (window.top && window.top !== window && window.top.opener) return window.top.opener; } catch (e) {}
  try { if (window.parent && window.parent !== window && window.parent.opener) return window.parent.opener; } catch (e) {}
  return null;
}
function erdoganZoomBroadcast(action, id) {
  var target = erdoganFindOpener();
  if (!target) return;
  try { target.postMessage({ erdoganZoom: true, action: action, id: id }, '*'); } catch (e) {}
}
function erdoganZoomOpen(id, fromMessage) {
  var overlay = document.getElementById(id);
  if (!overlay) return;
  // reveal.js applies a CSS transform (scale) to its .slides container
  // for responsive fit. A transformed ancestor becomes the containing
  // block for position:fixed descendants (and, combined with reveal's
  // own overflow:hidden, clips them), so a "fixed" overlay left inside
  // the slide tree renders squeezed into the slide's own box instead of
  // the real viewport. Moving it to <body> the first time it's opened
  // sidesteps that entirely.
  if (overlay.parentElement !== document.body) {
    document.body.appendChild(overlay);
  }
  overlay.classList.add('is-open');
  if (!fromMessage) erdoganZoomBroadcast('open', id);
}
function erdoganZoomClose(e, id, fromMessage) {
  if (e) {
    if (e.preventDefault) e.preventDefault();
    if (e.stopPropagation) e.stopPropagation();
  }
  var overlay = document.getElementById(id);
  if (overlay) overlay.classList.remove('is-open');
  if (!fromMessage) erdoganZoomBroadcast('close', id);
  return false;
}
function erdoganZoomMaybeClose(e, overlay) {
  if (e.target === overlay) {
    if (e) {
      if (e.preventDefault) e.preventDefault();
      if (e.stopPropagation) e.stopPropagation();
    }
    overlay.classList.remove('is-open');
    erdoganZoomBroadcast('close', overlay.id);
  }
}
window.addEventListener('message', function (e) {
  var data = e.data;
  if (!data) return;
  if (data.erdoganZoom) {
    if (data.action === 'open') erdoganZoomOpen(data.id, true);
    else erdoganZoomClose(null, data.id, true);
  } else if (data.erdoganNav) {
    erdoganNavTo(data.hash, true);
  } else if (data.erdoganCite) {
    erdoganCiteApply(data.id, data.action);
  }
});
// Same cross-window problem as the lightbox above, for the citation
// links Quarto's own citeproc output wires up ([@key] -> "(Author,
// Year)" linking to #/references): clicking one inside the speaker
// notes popup navigates only that popup's own reveal.js instance, so
// the slide jump is invisible to the audience on the real main window.
// Delegated at the document level (one listener) rather than per-link,
// since citation <a> tags are generated by pandoc/citeproc, not authored
// by hand, so there's no single place to attach an onclick="" to them.
function erdoganNavTo(hash, fromMessage) {
  if (!hash) return;
  if (location.hash !== hash) location.hash = hash;
  if (!fromMessage) {
    var target = erdoganFindOpener();
    if (target) {
      try { target.postMessage({ erdoganNav: true, hash: hash }, '*'); } catch (e) {}
    }
  }
}
document.addEventListener('click', function (e) {
  var link = e.target.closest && e.target.closest('a[role="doc-biblioref"]');
  if (!link) return;
  var href = link.getAttribute('href') || '';
  if (href.charAt(0) !== '#') return;
  erdoganNavTo(href, false);
});
// The citation tooltip itself (the little "(Author, Year)" popup with the
// reference text) is Quarto's own tippy.js hover tooltip, not something
// we click open -- same cross-window gap as everything above: hovering a
// citation inside the speaker notes popup shows tippy's popup only in
// that popup's own document, never on the real, audience-facing window.
// Every citation link gets a stable index (both windows load the exact
// same static HTML in the exact same DOM order, so index N always means
// the same citation on both sides); hovering broadcasts show/hide by
// index, and the receiving window drives that same-indexed link's own
// tippy instance (exposed by tippy.js as element._tippy) directly,
// rather than trying to reconstruct or move the tooltip's content.
function erdoganCiteBroadcast(id, action) {
  var target = erdoganFindOpener();
  if (!target) return;
  try { target.postMessage({ erdoganCite: true, id: id, action: action }, '*'); } catch (e) {}
}
function erdoganCiteApply(id, action) {
  var link = document.querySelector('a[role="doc-biblioref"][data-erdogan-cite-id="' + id + '"]');
  if (!link || !link._tippy) return;
  if (action === 'show') link._tippy.show(); else link._tippy.hide();
}
function erdoganCiteInit() {
  var links = document.querySelectorAll('a[role="doc-biblioref"]');
  links.forEach(function (link, i) {
    link.dataset.erdoganCiteId = i;
    link.addEventListener('mouseenter', function () { erdoganCiteBroadcast(i, 'show'); });
    link.addEventListener('mouseleave', function () { erdoganCiteBroadcast(i, 'hide'); });
    link.addEventListener('focus', function () { erdoganCiteBroadcast(i, 'show'); });
    link.addEventListener('blur', function () { erdoganCiteBroadcast(i, 'hide'); });
  });
}
// Deferred: Quarto's own script (which creates the tippy instances via
// tippyHover()) needs to have already run and attached ._tippy to each
// link before this reads it -- both run on window 'load', so a short
// timeout after load is a simple, reliable way to run after it.
window.addEventListener('load', function () { setTimeout(erdoganCiteInit, 150); });
document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
  if (e.key === 'Escape') {
    ['lb-circle', 'lb-sn1', 'lb-holepunch', 'lb-grid50', 'lb-grid100', 'lb-grid200', 'lb-grid400'].forEach(function (id) {
      var o = document.getElementById(id);
      if (o && o.classList.contains('is-open')) {
        o.classList.remove('is-open');
        erdoganZoomBroadcast('close', id);
      }
    });
  }
});
</script>

<div class="cmp-callout">Sample restricted to HR's exact <strong>126-country, 1992-2009</strong> window. Each column changes only the <strong>size and shape of the spatial unit</strong>, not the specification: from a tight 5&nbsp;km circle around the leader's birthplace, to the full home region, to the home region with the birth district cut out, to a world grid at four coarsening resolutions. The <strong>Leader coefficient shrinks toward zero as the unit gets larger</strong> in both HR's numbers and ours, the same pattern the paper reports: favoritism shows up most clearly close to the leader's birthplace and fades out as the unit of observation grows past it.</div>

::: {.notes}
This table changes the size of the spatial unit itself, not the
specification, so it leans on GIS work more than pure econometrics.

Column one draws a tight 5 kilometre circle around the leader's actual
birth coordinate. Our estimate comes out smaller and not significant here.

Column two is the home province as a full area average, and column three
is that same province with the leader's own birth district cut out of it,
and the coefficient drops from column two to column three the way HR
describe.

Columns four
through seven are the world grid, fifty up to four hundred kilometre
cells, and this is the cleanest replication in the table, the coefficient
shrinks steadily as the grid gets coarser and loses significance around
two hundred kilometres in both HR's numbers and ours.

So the pattern holds up independently, favoritism is strongest right at
the birthplace and fades out as the unit grows past it.
:::

<p class="cmp-footnote"><em>Notes.</em> Fixed effect regressions on the harmonized DMSP/VIIRS panel, 1992-2023 (except Column (5), which is standard OLS). Same seven specifications as the main replication's Table II, Columns (1)-(7); Column (8), which relies on G-Econ regional GDP, is not extended. Population is our own independently-built GHS-POP source. Standard errors clustered at the country level. \*\*\*, \*\*, \* indicate significance at the 1%, 5%, and 10% levels, respectively.</p>

<div class="cmp-callout">The core result <strong>holds up over the extended 1992-2023 window</strong>, using entirely our own extension-era data pipeline: the Leader coefficient is positive and significant across every specification, contemporaneous (Col 2), two-year lag (Col 3), the dynamic panel (Col 4), and the extensive margin (Col 6), the same pattern HR report in their own 1992-2009 window. Column (7)'s per-capita specification is the one exception, small and not significant, consistent with the same attenuation HR themselves see once population enters both sides of the ratio.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is Table II's own seven specifications, minus Column 8, re-estimated
end to end on our extension-era pipeline: the harmonized DMSP-VIIRS panel
running to 2023, and our own independently-built GHS-POP population
source wherever population enters.

The pattern holds up well. Column one, the baseline one-year lag, comes in
at 0.048, significant at five percent, actually a touch larger than HR's
own 1992-2009 estimate. Contemporaneous and two-year-lag versions in
columns two and three are close in magnitude and still significant.
Column four, the dynamic panel with lagged light on the right-hand side,
shows the coefficient shrink once persistence is controlled for, same
direction HR report. Column six, the extensive margin, stays significant.

Column seven is the honest exception: once light is expressed per capita
and population enters as its own control, the Leader effect shrinks to
essentially zero and loses significance. That is not a bug, it is the same
attenuation pattern HR's own paper shows in this specification, so it
strengthens rather than undermines confidence in the replication.
:::


# Conclusion {.section-slide visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.section-eyebrow}
Section 07 / 07
:::


## Conclusion {.content-slide}

### The replication holds

- HR 2014's central finding, that political leaders' birth regions receive brighter nighttime lights while they are in power, **reproduces cleanly** in our own independently-assembled data: same sign, same order of magnitude, across every geometric definition of "region" we tried, from a 5&nbsp;km circle to a 400&nbsp;km grid cell
- The few places our numbers diverge from HR's own (Table II Col 6, the Pop sign flip in Cols 7-8) trace to **documented, real source-vintage differences**, not construction bugs

### The extension confirms it, not just once

- The same Leader effect **survives an independently-rebuilt population pipeline** (GHS-POP) and a **32-year window** nearly double HR's original span, with the effect if anything slightly stronger
- Both the original replication and the extension land on the **same qualitative story**: birth-region favoritism in nighttime light is real, robust to spatial-unit choice, and not an artifact of any one data vintage or time window

::: {.notes}
So, pulling the whole talk together. The replication itself holds: HR's
central result, that a leader's home region lights up while they're in
power, reproduces cleanly across every geometric definition of region we
tried, circles, hole-punched provinces, grids at four resolutions, using
data we assembled entirely independently of HR's own files. The handful
of places our numbers diverge trace to specific, documented source-vintage
differences, not bugs in how we built the pipeline.

And the extension isn't a separate story, it's the same story tested a
second way. Swapping in our own independently-built population source and
nearly doubling the time window doesn't break the result, if anything the
effect is a touch stronger over the longer span. Two independent tests,
the geometric replication and the temporal extension, land on the same
answer: this is a real, robust pattern in the data, not a fragile artifact
of one specific choice HR happened to make in 2014.
:::
